findings.reason: ComponentTestBase.kt:22 takes `testScheduler` as a constructor parameter, and every subclass has to call `runTest(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))`. The argument is the base field and the name inside the lambda is TestScope's, which are the same object only because of that call pattern. waitUntil/tearDown use the base field. It works today, so this is a low maintainability point.
findings.claim: Passing the scheduler through the constructor is fragile, and the base-class field shadows TestScope.testScheduler. A test that uses plain runTest{} would silently drive a different clock.
findings.evidence: Every subclass passes a fresh `ComponentTestBase(TestCoroutineScheduler())`. The test bodies call `runTest(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { ... testScheduler.advanceTimeBy(...) }`, and inside that lambda `testScheduler` resolves to the TestScope receiver's property, not the base-class field. `waitUntil` and `tearDown` use the base-class field.

members.claim: Every subclass has to pass `TestCoroutineScheduler()` to the constructor, and each test has to remember to write `runTest(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))`. If a new test uses plain `runTest {}`, it gets a separate scheduler, and `waitUntil`/`tearDown` drive the wrong clock without any error. Create the scheduler inside the base class, and add a helper such as `fun runComponentTest(block: suspend TestScope.() -> Unit) = runTest(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), testBody = block)` so tests can't get this wrong.

findings.reason: ComponentTestBase.kt:526-532 does call advanceTimeBy(10) up to 500 times, and its KDoc says so. The default clientConfig uses pingPeriod 50s/pongWait 60s, so heartbeat timers don't fire within 5 s. Also, the old Dispatchers.Default poll ran inside runTest, which can auto-advance idle virtual time, so the claim that the old helper never moved virtual time is doubtful. No failing test is traced.
findings.claim: The new waitUntil advances virtual time by up to 5 s, which can fire client timers the test did not intend to fire and upset exact advanceTimeBy reasoning.
findings.evidence: The new `waitUntil` changes what the tests check. The old helper polled in real time and never moved virtual time. This one calls `testScheduler.advanceTimeBy(10)` up to 500 times, so it can silently move the clock forward by as much as 5s whenever the condition isn't already true. That fires any timer the client has queued, such as the pong deadline (`resetPongDeadline`), reconnect backoff (`reconnectLoop` delay) or ping loop delays. Tests like CallbackTest/ReconnectTest call `waitForPing` and then use exact `advanceTimeBy(5/20/50)` values to reason about backoff. If a wait doesn't succeed on the fast path, those timing assumptions break without any error, and timers can fire that the test never meant to fire. Prefer `testScheduler.runCurrent()` (no time change) or `advanceUntilIdle()` with a clear limit. At minimum, document that `waitUntil` moves virtual time and can fire client timers.

findings.reason: Tests do register testClient (21 assignments across the classes), so teardown does run close()/done.await() on clients bound to the test scheduler. The baseline teardown had the same hang risk, as the finding admits, and no specific test is shown to hang, so the regression isn't established.
findings.claim: tearDown runs runBlocking(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) after runTest has finished, which could hang forever if close() needs delayed scheduler tasks.
findings.evidence: `tearDown` now runs `runBlocking(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler))` after `runTest` has finished. Nothing advances the scheduler at that point. If `close()`/`done.await()` ever depends on a delayed or queued task on that scheduler (for example a client left mid-reconnect, or a test that never closes the client), teardown will block the JUnit thread forever with no timeout. The old version could also block, but it at least didn't tie teardown to a scheduler that has stopped running. The PR text says the client is always closed before teardown, but most tests don't close it and depend on teardown to do so. Consider adding a real-time `withTimeout` here, or closing the client inside `runTest`.
